# Learning R

In this section, one potentially new concept in R is introduced: writing own functions. It is later used to make the solutions more efficient. If we compute a number of values using expressions several times, programs can be made easier to read and modify by defining a new function. For example, we might want to compute the mean and standard deviation of several variables.

Here, we use the NECOSAD data as later used in this CP and compute mean/sd for variables `sf_phys0` and `age`. Note, that you have to replace the `myPath` given to `readRDS` with the location of the file on your computer (tutorial: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D1CpiGsXIS4)

```{r}
    myPath <- 'data/necosad.rds'    # <<- replace this
    data <- readRDS(myPath)
    # the parameter na.rm = TRUE removes missing values from the data
    mean_phy0 = mean(data$sf_phys0, na.rm = TRUE)
    sd_phy0 <- sd(data$sf_phys0, na.rm = TRUE)
    summ_phy0 <- c(mean_phy0, sd_phy0)

    mean_age <- mean(data$age, na.rm = TRUE)
    sd_age <- sd(data$age, na.rm = TRUE)
    summ_age <- c(mean_age, sd_age)

    print(rbind(summ_phy0, summ_age))
```

The same three lines are essentially repeated twice. A function is a shorthand for a number of expressions, which can be reused. We create a function by replacing the names that are different between blocks of code with a new name `x` (or another name, which can be chosen freely) and putting the new lines into the definition `functioname <- function(x) { lines_of_code }`. The same result as before can then be gotten by writing: `functioname(variable)`, where `variable` is the original value used such as `data$sf_phys0`.

```{r}
    varSummary <- function(x) {
        Mean <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
        Sd <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
        summ <- c(mean = Mean, sd = Sd)
    }
```
`varSummary` is a new function that can be used like the built-in R functions. The same result as above can now be achieved with the code:

```{r}
    print(rbind(phy0 = varSummary(data$sf_phys0), age = varSummary(data$age)))
```

# Part 1: Analysis of the NECOSAD data

NECOSAD is an observational prospective follow-up study in incidental dialysis patients starting either peritoneal or haemodialysis. At start of the study and at 6 months thereafter, various data were collected, including the patients’ physical activity score derived from a questionnaire.

In this computer practical, you will use linear regression analysis to test whether the physical activity at six months after start of dialysis is different between patients undergoing peritoneal as compared to haemodialysis.

## Q1: Describe the data

Use the dataset from the NECOSAD study loaded above (variable `data`).

How many patients are in the dataset, and how many and which percentage started with peritoneal or haemodialysis?

Hint: Use functions `dim` or `nrow`, function `table` to get counts, which can be converted to frequencies.

Number of patients:
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    nrow(data)
```
</div>

Proportions of type of therapy
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    table(data$therapy)/sum(table(data$therapy))
```
</div>

Create histograms for physical activity at baseline and after 6 month (function `hist`).
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    hist(data$sf_phys0)
```

```{r}
    hist(data$sf_phys6)
```
</div>

Create a table with baseline characteristics per therapy group.

Hint: use function `summary` for continuous and function `table` for categorical variables.

Function `by` can split an analysis by sub-groups. First develop R-code to show baseline charactersistics for the whole data set. Then the R-code `by(data, data$therapy, function(data) { your-code }` produces the desired result.

Use functions `mean`, `sd` to compute mean and standard deviation.

The code is given for continuous variables. Adapt the code to compute frequencies for categorical variables.

Baseline characteristics continuous variables:
```{r}
    by(data, data$therapy, function(data) {
        rbind(phy0 = varSummary(data$sf_phys0), age = varSummary(data$age))
    })
```

Baseline characteristics categorical variable (there is only `gender`).
You can use the following function `tableFreq <- function(x) { table(x)/sum(table(x)) }` to compute frequencies (it uses the `table` function to count levels and divides by the total).

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">

```{r}
    tableFreq <- function(x) { table(x)/sum(table(x)) }
    by(data, data$therapy, function(data) {
        rbind(tableFreq(data$gender))
    })
```
</div>

## Q2: Testing baseline variables

Test the baseline variables `sf_phys0`, `age` and `gender` for differences between the therapy groups.

Use the appropriate test. You can assume continuous variables to be normally distributed. Choose from functions (`t.test`, `chisq.test`).

`sf_phys0`
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    t.test(sf_phys0 ~ therapy, data)
```
</div>

`age`
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    t.test(age ~ therapy, data)
```
</div>

`gender`
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    table(data[, c('gender', 'therapy')])
    chisq.test(data$gender, data$therapy)
```
</div>

Draw conclusions from your results.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
Age and physical activity differ significantly at baseline between the groups. It is therefore likely that tretment choice is confounded by these or other variables. It seems that younger patients more frequenly undergo peritoneal dialysis. Sex distribution seems similar and might influence treament decision to a lesser degree than age.
</div>

## Q3: Physical Activity

Investigate the correlation between physical activity at baseline and 6 month. Use function `cor` to compute the correlation. Add the `use = 'pairwise.complete.obs'` argument to handle missing data.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    cor(data[, c('sf_phys0', 'sf_phys6')], use = 'pairwise.complete.obs')
```
The correlation is 0.71.
</div>

Test whether the correlation differs significantly form 0 with function `cor.test` and interpret your result.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
cor.test(~ sf_phys0 + sf_phys6, data = data)
```
The correlation is signficantly different from 0. This result is expected as baseline activity can hardly be independent of activity measured later even if other factors such as therapy have an influence as well.
</div>

Create a scatter plot for the two activity measurements. Use `ggplot` from package `ggplot2` as follows: `ggplot(data, aes(x = sf_phys0, y = sf_phys6)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)`

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    library(ggplot2)
    ggplot(data = data, aes(x = sf_phys0, y = sf_phys6)) + 
      geom_point() +
      geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```
</div>

## Q4: Phusical activity and groups

Compare physical activity at 6 months between therapy groups. Use the appropriate test. Again, you can assume continuous variables to be normally distributed.

`sf_phys6`
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
    t.test(sf_phys6 ~ therapy, data)
```
</div>

Which conclusions can you draw?
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
The difference is statistically significant. The haemodialysis group reports lower activity scores than the peritonal group. However, this analysis does not account for potential confounding.
</div>

What is the minimal, statistically significant difference between the therapy groups according to the confidence interval for the difference (at the 95% significance level)?
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
The upper bound reported from the t-test is -7.96 and represents this difference.
</div>

## Q5: Effect of age and gender

Investigate the influence of `age` and `gender` on physical activity separately at 6 month using linear regression.

Hint: Use `summary(lm(formula, data))` for your analyses.

`age`

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(sf_phys6 ~ age, data))
```
</div>

`gender`

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(sf_phys6 ~ gender, data))
```
</div>

Use `gender` and `age` simultaneously in the regression:

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(sf_phys6 ~ age + gender, data))
```
</div>

Interpret your results.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
Age and gender separately have signficant effects. Higher age and being female corresponds to lower physical activity. The analysis of both variables together shows that these effects are independent, i.e. they are not explained by correlation between the variables. Regression coefficients stay roughly the same when comparing the analyses, implying the there is almost no confounding between the variables.
</div>

## Q6: Research question

Answer the research question with a linear regression of activity at 6 month regressed on therapy and age.

Start by not adding any covariate, then adding only age or gender and finally both. Therapy should always be in the model (variable of interest).

Start by only including `therapy`. Interpret the regression coefficient for therapy.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(sf_phys6 ~ therapy, data))
```

The regression coefficient is the same as the difference reported for the t-test. A linear regression with a single, binary covariate is the same as a t-test. The t-test is therefore a special case of a linear regression.
</div>

Also include `gender` in the analysis.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(sf_phys6 ~ gender + therapy, data))
```

The regression coefficient of therapy is almost unchanged as compared to the previous analysis. This confirms, that sex dos not seem to be a confounder in the acitivty/therypy relationship.
</div>

`age`
**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(sf_phys6 ~ age + therapy, data))
```
</div>

Interpret your result.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
The regression coefficient of therapy is roughly halfed as compared to the first analysis. This confirms a potential role of age as a confounder in the acitivty/therypy relationship.
</div>

Use `gender` and `age` together in the regression:

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(sf_phys6 ~ age + gender + therapy, data))
```
</div>

Interpret your result.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
The regression coefficient of therapy is roughly the same as in the previous analysis. Again, gender does not seem to act as a confounder in the acitivty/therypy relationship.
</div>

## Q7: Physical activity corrected for baseline activity

Run a linear regression of activity at 6 month regressed on therapy, age, gender and baseline activity.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(sf_phys6 ~ sf_phys0 + age + gender + therapy, data))
```
</div>

Interpret your result.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
The regression coefficient of therapy is now 1.2 and no longer statistically significant. Gender is no longer statistically significant as compared to previous models. The significant covariates are age and baseline physical activity.
</div>

What type of confounding is the analysis compatible with?

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
The results suggest that age and baseline activity could have influenced the selection of study arm. Younger and more active patients are more often treated with peritoneal dialysis. This could be a preference by the patients themselves as peritoneal dialysis can be given at home whereas haemodialysis requires treatment in the hospital. This interpretation would be confounding by indication.
</div>

Give a conclusion from the analysis of the data.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
The mode of treatment (peritoneal vs. haemodialysis) does not significantly influence physical activity at 6 month. Differences between the groups are most likely due to differences in age and baseline activity as selected for the modes of treatment.
</div>

# Part 2: Analysis of pea data

Load the data set with

```{r}
    myPathNpk <- 'data/npk.rds'     # <<- needs to be changed
    data <- readRDS(myPathNpk)
```

The data set is about an agricultural experiment where the yield of pea plants is studied when plants are exposed to nitrogen, phosphate or potassium. The columns N, P, K are binary variables (yes/no variables) indicating whether nitrogen, phosphate or potassium have been applied, respectively. Yield is the outcome measurement of pea fruits in grams. The variable block indicates on which plot (location) the plant grew.

Finally, the variable ‘combination’ contains which combination of N, P and K was used for the plant.

## Q1: Insepct the data

Use the Rstudio data view or type `data` in the console.

## Q2: Linear regression

Run a linear regression with dependent variable `yield` and independent variable `combination`.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(yield ~ combination, data))
```
</div>

What does row `(Intercept)` and the other values in the `Estimate` column represent? What is the interpretation of the column `Pr(>|t|)`? 

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
`(Intercept)` represents the mean yield in the reference group, i.e. `N;noP;K`. The other values in column `Estimate` represent the difference of the mean yield in the other groups with the reference group.  Column `Pr(>|t|)` gives P-values for whether the differences are unequal  to zero. For `(Intercept)` the P-value corresponds to the null-hypothesis that the intercept is 0.
No factor level leads to a yield that is significantly different from the reference level. The intercept is significanctly different from 0.
</div>

## Q3: Create dummy variables manually

The variables listed in the output table above are dummy variables which were derived from the variable ‘combination’ by R. Create these dummy variables manually.

The following R-code creates a 0-1 dummy vector for factor level 2 (`N;noP;noK`).
```{r}
lvls = levels(data$combination)
lv2 = lvls[2]
dummy2 = as.numeric(data$combination == lv2)
```

Check whether this vector has a 1 when the factor level is present and 0 otherwise.

```{r}
cbind(data, dummy2)
```

Use the following code to create all dummy variables.
```{r}
allDummies = sapply(lvls, function(lv)as.numeric(data$combination == lv))
```

Check correctness by inspecting a few rows of the following data frame:
```{r}
data.frame(data$combination, allDummies)
```

## Q4: Run the regression

Run a regression analysis with yield as covariate and the new dummy variables as covariates.

```{r}
    data2 = data.frame(yield = data$yield, allDummies)
```

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(yield ~ ., data2))
```
The `.` on the right-hand side indicates that all variables except the outcome should be used as covariates.
</div>

Why do you see a row with `NA` values?

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
When performing a linear regression with a factor as a covariate, R chooses a reference category (level). The mean value of this category is reported as the intercept and all other effects are the difference with this refernence value. As we included all categories (levels) as separate columns in the linear regression, this time one column has to be chosen as reference category. R always reports output for all provided columns (covariates) but sets values to `NA` if values cannot be computed (for example, when the covariate corresponds to the reference category). 
</div>

Remove the first dummy variable corresponding to level `N;noP;K`. This can be done by using a negative column index: `allDummies[, -1]`.

```{r}
    data3 = data.frame(yield = data$yield, allDummies[, -1])
```

Rerun the analysis and describe results.

**fillin**:  
<div class="answer">
```{r}
summary(lm(yield ~ ., data3))
```

The `NA`s have disappeared. Also no row for `N;noP;K` is reported. By removing this column, we have explicitly chosen this factor level as the reference category.
</div>

What are the group means for combinations `noN;noP;noK`, `noN;P;K`, and `noN;P;noK`? Use the output from the previous question (Parameter estimates/Coefficients) to compute the values.

**fillin**:  

<div class="answer">
```{r}
    cfs = coefficients(summary(lm(yield ~ ., data3)))
    cfs['(Intercept)', 'Estimate'] + cfs['noN.noP.noK', 'Estimate']
    cfs['(Intercept)', 'Estimate'] + cfs['noN.P.K', 'Estimate']
    cfs['(Intercept)', 'Estimate'] + cfs['noN.P.noK', 'Estimate']
```
The code above performs the computations directly from the linear regression. The values can also be numerically read off of the output.
</div>

Compare the result from the model `lm(yield ~ ., data3)` (above) with the model `lm(yield ~ combination, data)` (Q1). Interpret.

**fillin**:  

<div class="answer">
The output is identical. When R includes a factor into a regression, the same steps as for generating `data3` are taken internally. In addition, R chooses the first level as reference category.
</div>
